q: The 'Udyam' registration for micro, small and medium enterprises replaced the earlier registration system with effect from:
options: 1 April 2018
1 January 2019
1 July 2020
1 April 2021
explanation: The revised MSME classification came into force on 1 July 2020, and the Udyam registration portal replaced the earlier Udyog Aadhaar and permanent account number based registration for MSMEs.

q: Under the revised MSME classification, an enterprise in the manufacturing sector is a 'micro' enterprise if its investment in plant and machinery is up to:
options: Rs 1 crore
Rs 2.5 crore
Rs 10 crore
Rs 5 crore
explanation: A micro manufacturing enterprise has an investment of up to Rs 2.5 crore and turnover of up to Rs 10 crore, a small enterprise has investment up to Rs 25 crore and turnover up to Rs 100 crore, and a medium enterprise has investment up to Rs 125 crore and turnover up to Rs 500 crore.

q: The incentives under the Production Linked Incentive schemes introduced in 2020 are generally payable for a period of:
options: ten years
three years
seven years
five years with an option to extend
explanation: The PLI schemes for the 14 sectors offer incentives for five years from the date of commercial production, with an option to extend the scheme by a further three years on the basis of performance.

q: The 'TReDS' platform in India is used for:
options: the settlement of retail payments on the UPI platform
the electronic tendering of defence equipment
on-line disclosure and settlement of invoices of micro and small enterprises through a network of buyers and financiers
the trading of carbon credits
explanation: TReDS, or the Trade Receivables Discounting System, is an online exchange that allows MSMEs to upload invoices and lets buyers and financiers discount them, thereby easing working capital stress.

q: The National MSME Policy was announced in:
explanation: The National MSME Policy, notified in 2020, aimed at raising the contribution of micro, small and medium enterprises to GDP and exports, with targets for employment, productivity and formalisation.

q: The 'Delayed Payment to Micro and Small Enterprises' Act was enacted in:
explanation: The MSMED Act, 2006 was the first legislation to provide for a statutory mechanism for MSME buyers to pay their suppliers on time, with compensation for delayed payment and a buyer as a fit and proper person.

q: The 'Startup India' mission was launched in:
explanation: Startup India, launched on 16 August 2016, created a separate ministry department for startup recognition, a fund of funds, and a tax exemption for recognised startups under section 115-I of the Income Tax Act.

q: The income tax exemption for recognised startups in India is provided under which section of the Income Tax Act, 1961?
options: Section 35D
Section 80-I
Section 115-I
Section 10(23D)
explanation: Section 115-I allows a deduction of the eligible expenditure of eligible startups recognised by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, and section 80-I covers eligible startups in the services sector.

q: The 'National Career Service' portal is operated by:
options: the Ministry of Labour and Employment
the National Skill Development Corporation
the Ministry of Education
NITI Aayog
explanation: The National Career Service, a Ministry of Labour and Employment initiative, provides an online platform for job seekers, employers and skill providers with a common platform for career counselling and job matching.

q: The 'Skill India' programme was launched in:
explanation: Skill India was launched in July 2015 with the aim of skilling one person in every household and giving at least one woman in every household a source of livelihood, through partnerships with the private sector.

q: The National Skill Development Corporation is a:
options: statutory regulator of vocational training
division of the National Apprenticeship Board
public sector undertaking owned by state governments
not-for-profit company set up by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship
explanation: NSDC is a not-for-profit company limited by shares under the Companies Act, set up by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship to catalyse and support skill building in the country.

q: The 'National Single Window' system for industrial clearances is operated by:
options: the Ministry of Commerce and Industry
the Reserve Bank of India
the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
explanation: The National Single Window portal is an online platform of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry that allows a business to apply for licences, permits and approvals across ministries and states on a single form.

q: The Quality Control Order of the Bureau of Indian Standards makes certification compulsory for products such as:
options: all electronic goods sold online
toys, cement and a growing list of other products
only imported steel products
only packaged drinking water
explanation: BIS Quality Control Orders made the ISI mark mandatory for a specified list of products, beginning with toys and cement and later extended to items such as electrical fittings, gas cylinders and helmets.

q: The Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules require a packaged commodity to carry a declaration of:
options: the maximum retail price and the tax identification number
the ingredients, the batch number and the expiry date only
the net quantity, maximum retail price, manufacturer or packer and the month and year of packing
only the net quantity and the barcode
explanation: The rules require the manufacturer or packer, the net quantity in the prescribed unit, the maximum retail price, the month and year of packing, the consumer care details and the last date of use for applicable commodities to be displayed on the package.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three pillars of the 'Make in India' programme launched in 2014?
options: new infrastructure
increasing the level of agricultural subsidies
skill development
new manufacturing
explanation: Make in India was built on three pillars, namely skill development, new manufacturing and new infrastructure; raising agricultural subsidies was never part of its framework.

q: Small finance banks in India are required to extend at least what percentage of their credit to the priority sector?
options: 75 per cent
50 per cent
18 per cent
40 per cent
explanation: Small finance banks must extend 75 per cent of their adjusted net bank credit to the priority sector, of which 40 per cent must be for agriculture and allied activities and at least 5 per cent for weaker sections.

q: The Immediate Payment Service (IMPS) was launched in India in:
explanation: IMPS, operated by the National Payments Corporation of India, was launched in 2010 as a 24x7 system for instant transfer of funds, while the UPI was launched in 2016 and RuPay in 2012.

q: The 'RuPay' card was launched in India in:
explanation: RuPay was launched in 2012 by the National Payments Corporation of India as a domestic payment card system that operates on the lines of Visa and Mastercard.

q: Under the RBI's Prompt Corrective Action framework, a bank has to report to the RBI when its net non-performing asset ratio exceeds:
options: 5 per cent
10 per cent
2 per cent
8 per cent
explanation: Under the PCA framework a bank is placed under restrictions if its net NPA exceeds 5 per cent, or if its capital to risk-weighted assets ratio falls below the prescribed threshold without new capital being raised.

q: The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation insures bank deposits up to:
options: Rs 1 lakh
Rs 5 lakh
Rs 2 lakh
Rs 10 lakh
explanation: DICGC, a wholly owned subsidiary of the RBI, insures bank deposits up to Rs 5 lakh per depositor per bank, and the insurance premium is paid by the banks themselves.

q: The 'Account Aggregator' framework in India works as:
options: a mandatory sharing of customer data by all banks with the tax department
a system of compulsory credit reporting to the Credit Information Companies
a mechanism for the RBI to ration credit among banks
a consent-based financial information system operated by registered account aggregators with a consent manager
explanation: The Account Aggregator ecosystem, built under the RBI's Financial Information (Account Aggregator) Regulations, lets a customer share financial data from multiple financial information providers with a consent manager in a standardised, secure manner.

q: A grant received by a State Government from the central government is regarded as:
options: a revenue receipt of the State, not a capital receipt
a capital receipt of the State
neither revenue nor capital
a capital receipt only if it is tied to a construction project
explanation: Grants are treated as revenue receipts of the recipient government, whether or not they are tied to a specific project, which is why they are not counted as capital receipts or as borrowings.

q: The 'effective revenue deficit' was introduced in Indian fiscal accounting to:
options: measure the fiscal deficit of the States on a cash basis
compute the revenue deficit including the receipts of the Public Account
compute the revenue deficit after deducting the interest payments of the States
measure the revenue deficit excluding the capital expenditure component that is financed by market borrowings
explanation: The effective revenue deficit deducts from the revenue deficit the capital expenditure of the States that is met through market borrowings, giving a truer picture of the revenue demand on the States' own resources.

q: Interest payments on the public debt of the central government are classified as:
options: capital expenditure
revenue receipt
revenue expenditure with no tax implications
capital receipt
explanation: Interest on borrowed funds is a revenue expenditure but it has no tax implications because it is a contractual payment on past borrowing and is not a fresh claim on current resources.

q: The 'Outcome Budget' in India was introduced with the objective of:
options: linking the fiscal deficit target with the inflation target
linking budget outlays with the outputs to be delivered and the outcomes to be achieved
replacing the annual budget with a five-year rolling plan
consolidating the railway and general budgets
explanation: The Outcome Budget builds on the 2019-20 attempt to link expenditure with outcomes for schemes of the ministries, so that the annual budget becomes a statement of measurable deliverables rather than of inputs alone.

q: Zero-based budgeting in India implies:
options: the budget is prepared by the states and not by the Union
only new schemes are funded and old schemes are automatically discontinued
expenditure is frozen at the previous year's level
every year's expenditure is reviewed afresh without regard to the previous year's allocations
explanation: Zero-based budgeting treats each year's allocation as a fresh exercise, requiring every scheme to justify its outlay in the light of the year's priorities rather than simply carrying forward the previous year's provision.

q: The 'escape clause' under the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act permits the government to:
options: deviate from the fiscal deficit target in exceptional circumstances such as national security, natural calamities or a collapse in farm output
waive interest payments on the public debt
abolish the Consolidated Fund of India
raise the fiscal deficit target beyond 3 per cent without any parliamentary approval
explanation: The escape clause allows the government to depart from the FRBM targets in exceptional circumstances and also enables deviation from the recommended fiscal deficit path if the macro-economic situation demands it.

q: The Consolidated Fund of a State is operated by:
options: the Comptroller and Auditor General
the Governor of the State
the Chief Minister of the State
the Union Finance Minister
explanation: Article 266 provides for the Consolidated Fund of each State to be operated by the Governor, either in his own charge or in the charge of officers appointed by him in writing.

q: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 applies to establishments employing:
options: 5 or more employees
50 or more employees
10 or more employees
20 or more employees
explanation: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 applies to every establishment in the private or public sector employing 10 or more persons, and the payment becomes payable on resignation, retirement, death or disablement.

q: The 'Minimum Wages Act, 1948' is administered by:
options: the National Labour Commission
the concerned State Government
the Central Government alone
the Reserve Bank of India
explanation: The Minimum Wages Act is administered by the State Governments through their labour departments, and the Central Government fixes the minimum wages for certain central government undertakings.

q: The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 provides for:
options: the machinery of conciliation, arbitration and adjudication of industrial disputes
the certification of fair wages
the registration of employment exchanges
the regulation of trade union finances
explanation: The Industrial Disputes Act sets out the procedure for the settlement of industrial disputes through conciliation, arbitration or adjudication by the appropriate authority, and also provides for the strike and lock-out machinery.

q: The 'Code on Wages, 2019' fixes the wage ceiling for contributions to the Employees' Provident Fund and the Employees' State Insurance at:
options: Rs 25,000 per month
Rs 21,000 per month
Rs 10,000 per month
Rs 15,000 per month
explanation: The Code on Wages, 2019 rationalises the wage structure and fixes the monthly wage ceiling for EPF and ESIC coverage at Rs 15,000, replacing the earlier separate limits of Rs 15,000 and Rs 21,000.

q: Under the Trade Unions Act, 1926, a trade union must be formed by at least:
options: two-thirds of the workers of an industry
fifteen members of the same establishment
seven members, of whom at least two-thirds must be employed in the same industry
ten members from the same industry
explanation: Section 4 of the Trade Unions Act requires at least seven persons to form a union, of whom at least two-thirds must be employed in the same industry for the union to qualify for the Act's benefits.

q: The 'Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976' is administered by the:
options: National Human Rights Commission
Ministry of Labour and Employment in consultation with the State Governments
Ministry of Home Affairs
Ministry of Rural Development
explanation: The Act is administered by the central government in consultation with the State Governments, with district Vigilance Committees inspecting and reporting on the working of the Act, and the offence of bonded labour is cognizable.

q: The 'Code on Social Security, 2020' provides for:
options: the merger of the EPF and ESI organisations
a fixed wage ceiling for all social security contributions
the abolition of the Employees' Provident Fund
a wider coverage of workers including gig and platform workers and the creation of a National Social Security Board
explanation: The Code on Social Security, 2020 widens the definition of workers to include gig and platform workers, provides for a National Social Security Board and an aggregator, and creates a framework for voluntary and assisted registration of gig workers.

q: The 'Import-Export Policy' of India is administered by the:
options: the Reserve Bank of India
the Ministry of Finance
the Directorate General of Foreign Trade under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry
the Export-Import Bank of India
explanation: The Directorate General of Foreign Trade administers the Import-Export Policy, issues licences and also administers the export promotion schemes such as RoDTEP, while the RBI regulates the foreign exchange aspects.

q: The 'Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999' replaced which earlier statute?
options: the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1974
the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
the Companies Act, 1956
the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
explanation: FEMA 1999, which came into force in May 1999, replaced the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1974 and shifted the approach from discretionary control of foreign exchange to management, with the goal of promoting orderly foreign exchange markets.

q: The 'errors and omissions' component in India's Balance of Payments mainly arises because of:
options: the depreciation of the rupee
the accumulation of foreign exchange reserves
unrecorded private transactions and gaps in the statistical data
profits remitted by foreign companies
explanation: Because trade and capital flows are recorded from different returns, unrecorded transactions and timing differences appear as errors and omissions, and the component is a residual that tends to be small over the long run.

q: In India's Balance of Payments, inward workers' remittances are recorded under:
options: secondary income in the current account
the financial account
capital transfers in the capital account
primary income in the current account
explanation: Remittances from Indians working abroad are unrequited transfers and are therefore shown as secondary income in the current account, which is one of the largest contributors to India's current account balance.

q: The 'RoDTEP' scheme provides:
options: a rebate on customs duty for imports
remission of embedded taxes to exporters, replacing the duty drawback and focus product schemes
a mandatory export obligation for domestic companies
an interest subsidy on export credit
explanation: The Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products scheme scrip-based mechanism allows exporters to claim back embedded taxes, replacing the earlier duty drawback and focus product schemes with a single consolidated scheme.

q: A 'Special Rupee Vostro' account is used for:
options: holding foreign exchange reserves of the RBI
parking foreign direct investment inflows of Indian companies
financing imports through the Export-Import Bank
settling trade transactions with a designated foreign agency by converting rupee balances into the currency of that country
explanation: Special Rupee Vostro accounts are opened by the RBI for foreign countries or their agencies to enable them to trade with India and convert the rupee balances into their own currency at the designated rate.

q: In a perfectly competitive market, the equilibrium price is determined where:
options: the government fixes the price equal to average cost
demand is perfectly inelastic
market demand equals market supply
the marginal cost of the single firm equals the market price
explanation: Under perfect competition the market price is determined by the interaction of aggregate demand and aggregate supply, and each firm is a price taker that equates its own marginal cost with that market price.

q: The 'law of increasing returns to a variable factor' applies when:
options: all factors of production are variable in the long run
all other factors are held constant in the short run
the size of the firm is fixed in the long run
there is perfect competition in the product market
explanation: Returns to a variable factor are a short-run concept in which one input is varied while the others are fixed, and diminishing returns set in when the marginal product of the variable factor starts falling.

q: In the Indian national accounts, 'gross value added' at basic prices includes:
options: the value of all final goods and services at market prices
the value of output minus depreciation
the total income of all factor owners after taxes
the value of output minus intermediate consumption, including taxes on production but excluding subsidies
explanation: GVA at basic prices is output at basic prices less intermediate consumption, and the sum of GVA across all industries gives GDP at market prices, which is why the two are reconciled in the national accounts.

q: The expenditure approach to estimating GDP is employed mainly because:
options: data on production by industry are not available or adequate for a detailed estimate
it is the only method that captures the contribution of the services sector
it is the method prescribed for computing per capita income
it allows the state to correct the estimate of the base year
explanation: While the production or income approach is preferred for the official estimates in India, the expenditure approach is used when production data are inadequate, and it also serves as a check on the consistency of the other two approaches.

q: In the national accounts, depreciation of fixed assets is also termed as:
options: consumption of fixed capital
gross capital formation
net value added at factor cost
reserve for depreciation
explanation: Consumption of fixed capital is the fall in the value of fixed assets due to wear, obsolescence and accidental damage, and deducting it from gross value added gives net value added.

q: The 'Competition Commission of India' can impose a monetary penalty for abuse of dominance up to:
options: 25 per cent of the total turnover of the market
1 per cent of the turnover of the dominant undertaking
5 per cent of the annual profit of the company
10 per cent of the total turnover or assets of the undertaking
explanation: Under section 7 of the Competition Act, 2002 the Commission may impose a penalty of up to 10 per cent of the total turnover or assets of the undertaking for abuse of dominance, and twice that amount for a repeat offence.

q: Under the 'Minimum Export Price' mechanism, an exporter must export at a price not below the price notified by:
options: the Ministry of Agriculture
the Directorate General of Foreign Trade
the Commodity Futures Market regulator
the Reserve Bank of India
explanation: The Ministry of Commerce notifies Minimum Export Prices for specified items such as onions and certain varieties of rice through the DGFT, and exports below the notified price are penalised under the export policy.

q: Which of the following is a correct statement about India's Public Investment Borrowing through Government securities?
options: The central government does not borrow from international markets at all
All borrowing is done through the Reserve Bank of India as the sole banker to the government
The share of the budget deficit financed through market borrowings has risen steadily while the share of cash balances has declined
Government securities are never auctioned to the public
explanation: Since the fiscal consolidation roadmap, a rising share of the central government's net borrowing has been met through market issues of government securities, with the cash balance component deliberately reduced to keep the deficit within the target.
